items.stem: In the example of an athlete running back and forth on a straight track as shown in the figure, when will the displacement of the athlete be zero? What will be the total distance travelled in that case?
items.answer: The displacement of the athlete will be zero when they return to their initial starting point O. In this case, since the athlete ran from point O to point A (100 m) and then all the way back to point O (100 m), the total distance travelled will be 200 m.

items.stem: Fuel used up in a vehicle depends on which of the following? Justify your answer. (i) Total distance travelled (ii) Displacement
items.answer: Fuel used up in a vehicle depends on the (i) total distance travelled. This is because the engine must continuously burn fuel to generate energy for every part of the physical path the vehicle moves along, regardless of its direction. Even if a vehicle returns to its starting point resulting in a net displacement of zero, fuel has been constantly consumed throughout the journey to cover the actual distance driven.

items.stem: A ball rolls down an inclined track as shown in Figure. Is its motion a straight line motion? Assuming the starting point of the ball (O) to be the origin, can its motion from O to D be depicted using a horizontal line as shown in Figure? Are the values of total distance travelled and magnitude of displacement from O equal or different at positions A, B, C and D?
items.answer: Yes, the motion of the ball rolling down the inclined track is a straight line motion because it follows a single linear path downwards. Assuming the starting point O is the origin, its motion can easily be depicted using a horizontal line by simply defining the positive direction along the track and mapping the linear measurements to a straight horizontal axis. Furthermore, because the ball continuously moves in only one forward direction without turning back, the values of total distance travelled and the magnitude of displacement from O will be exactly equal at all positions A, B, C, and D.

items.stem: Under what condition(s) is the (i) magnitude of average velocity of an object equal to its average speed? (ii) magnitude of average velocity of an object zero while its average speed is not zero?
items.answer: (i) The magnitude of average velocity is equal to average speed only when an object moves in a straight line in a single direction without ever turning back, ensuring that the total distance travelled perfectly equals the magnitude of displacement. (ii) The average velocity is zero while the average speed is not zero when an object completes a journey where its final position is the same as its starting position. In this scenario, the overall displacement is zero, but the object has still covered a measurable total distance during its movement.

items.stem: My father went to a shop from home which is located at a distance of 250 m on a straight road. On reaching there, he discovered that he forgot to carry a cloth bag. He came home to take it, went to the shop again, bought provisions and came back home. How much was the total distance travelled by him? What was his displacement from home?
items.answer: The total distance travelled is the sum of all the path lengths covered. He went to the shop (250 m), came back home (250 m), went to the shop again (250 m), and finally came back home (250 m). Total distance = 250 + 250 + 250 + 250 = 1000 m. Since his initial position (home) and final position (home) are the same, the net change in his position is zero. Therefore, his displacement from home is 0 m.

items.stem: A student runs from the ground floor to the fourth floor of a school building to collect a book and then comes down to their classroom on the second floor. If the height of each floor is 3 m, find: (i) the total vertical distance travelled, and (ii) their displacement from the starting point.
items.answer: (i) The student travels up 4 floors (ground to 4th) and then down 2 floors (4th to 2nd). Total floors covered = 4 + 2 = 6 floors. Total vertical distance travelled = 6 floors × 3 m/floor = 18 m. (ii) Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between the initial and final positions. The starting point is the ground floor (0 m) and the final point is the second floor (2 floors × 3 m = 6 m high). Therefore, the displacement is 6 m upwards from the starting point.

items.stem: A girl is riding her scooter and finds that its speedometer reading is constant. Is it possible for her scooter to be accelerating and if so, how?
items.answer: Yes, it is possible for the scooter to be accelerating even if the speedometer reading (which measures only speed) is constant. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and velocity has both magnitude (speed) and direction. If the girl is riding her scooter along a circular or curved path at a constant speed, the direction of her motion is continuously changing. This continuous change in direction means her velocity is changing, which results in the scooter accelerating.

items.stem: A car starts from rest and its velocity reaches 24 m s-1 in 6 s. Find the average acceleration and the distance travelled in these 6 s.
items.answer: Given: initial velocity u = 0 m s-1 (starts from rest); final velocity v = 24 m s-1; time t = 6 s. (i) Average acceleration: a = (v − u)/t = (24 − 0)/6 = 4 m s-2. (ii) Distance travelled, using the first equation of motion: s = ut + (1/2)at² = (0)(6) + (1/2)(4)(6)² = 0 + 2 × 36 = 72 m.

items.stem: A motorbike moving with initial velocity 28 m s-1 and constant acceleration stops after travelling 98 m. Find the acceleration of the motorbike and the time taken to come to a stop.
items.answer: Given: initial velocity u = 28 m s-1; final velocity v = 0 m s-1 (comes to a stop); distance s = 98 m. (i) Acceleration, using the equation of motion v² = u² + 2as: 0² = 28² + 2 × a × 98, so 0 = 784 + 196a, giving 196a = −784 and a = −784/196 = −4 m s-2. The negative sign indicates deceleration (retardation). (ii) Time taken, using the equation of motion v = u + at: 0 = 28 + (−4)t, so 4t = 28 and t = 28/4 = 7 s.

items.stem: Figure shows a position-time graph of two objects A and B that are moving along the parallel tracks in the same direction. Do objects A and B ever have equal velocity? Justify your answer.
items.answer: Based on the position-time graph in the figure, objects A and B do not ever have equal velocity. The velocity of an object is given by the slope of its position-time graph. Since the graphs for both objects are straight lines, they are moving with constant velocities. However, the line for object A is steeper than the line for object B, indicating that the slope of A is greater than the slope of B. Because their slopes (velocities) are constant and different from each other throughout the motion, they never have equal velocity.

items.stem: A graph in figure shows the change in position with time for two objects A and B moving in a straight line from 0 to 10 seconds. Choose the correct option(s). (i) The average velocity of both over the 10 s time interval is equal since they have the same initial and final positions. (ii) The average speeds of both over the 10 s time interval are equal since both cover equal distance in equal time. (iii) The average speed of A over the 10 s time interval is lower than that of B since it covers a shorter distance than B in 10 seconds. (iv) The average speed of A over the 10 s time interval is greater than that of B since B’s speed is lower than A’s in some segments.
items.answer: The correct options are (i) and (ii). According to the graph, both objects start at position 0 at time 0 s and end at the exact same position at time 10 s. Since their initial and final positions are identical, their net displacements are equal. Dividing this equal displacement by the same 10 s time interval gives equal average velocities, confirming option (i). Furthermore, because both objects move in a straight line in one direction without turning back (position only increases), their total distance travelled is equal to the magnitude of their displacement. Since both covered equal total distance in the same time, their average speeds are also equal, confirming option (ii).

items.stem: A truck driver driving at the speed of 54 km h-1 notices a road sign with a speed limit of 40 km h-1 for trucks. He slows down to 36 km h-1 in 36 s. What was the distance travelled by him during this time? Assume the acceleration to be constant while slowing down.
items.answer: Given: initial velocity u = 54 km h-1; final velocity v = 36 km h-1; time t = 36 s. Converting km h-1 to m s-1 (multiply by 5/18): u = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m s-1; v = 36 × 5/18 = 10 m s-1. Distance travelled, using the equation of motion s = ((u + v)/2) × t: s = ((15 + 10)/2) × 36 = (25/2) × 36 = 12.5 × 36 = 450 m.

items.stem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 20 m s-1 in 5 seconds. It then travels at 20 m s-1 for 10 seconds and finally applies the brake (with uniform acceleration) to stop in 6 seconds. Find the total distance travelled.
items.answer: The journey has three phases. Phase I — acceleration (u = 0, v = 20 m s-1, t = 5 s), using s = ((u + v)/2) × t: s1 = ((0 + 20)/2) × 5 = 10 × 5 = 50 m. Phase II — constant velocity (v = 20 m s-1, t = 10 s), using s = v × t: s2 = 20 × 10 = 200 m. Phase III — deceleration (u = 20 m s-1, v = 0, t = 6 s), using s = ((u + v)/2) × t: s3 = ((20 + 0)/2) × 6 = 10 × 6 = 60 m. Total distance S = s1 + s2 + s3 = 50 + 200 + 60 = 310 m.

items.stem: A bus is travelling at 36 km h-1 when the driver sees an obstacle 30 m ahead. The driver takes 0.5 seconds to react before pressing the brake. Once the brake is applied, the velocity of the bus reduces with constant acceleration of 2.5 m s-2. Will the bus be able to stop before reaching the obstacle?
items.answer: Given: initial speed u = 36 km h-1 = 10 m s-1; obstacle distance d = 30 m; reaction time tr = 0.5 s; deceleration a = 2.5 m s-2. Unit conversion: u = 36 × 5/18 = 10 m s-1. Phase I — reaction distance (no braking yet, constant speed), using s = u × t: s1 = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m. Phase II — braking distance (u = 10 m s-1, v = 0, a = −2.5 m s-2), using v² = u² + 2as so that s = (v² − u²)/(2a): s2 = (0² − 10²)/(2 × −2.5) = −100/−5 = 20 m. Total stopping distance S = s1 + s2 = 5 + 20 = 25 m. Since 25 m is less than the 30 m to the obstacle, the bus is able to stop before reaching it.

items.stem: A student said, “The Earth moves around the Sun”. In this context, discuss whether an object kept on the Earth can be considered to be at rest.
items.answer: Motion is a relative concept, meaning whether an object is at rest or in motion depends on the observer’s frame of reference. An object kept on the Earth is at rest with respect to the Earth itself, because its position relative to the Earth’s surface does not change with time. However, if that same object is observed from the perspective of the Sun or from space, it is in continuous motion because it revolves around the Sun along with the Earth. Therefore, the object can be considered at rest relative to the Earth, but it is simultaneously in motion relative to the Sun.

items.stem: Rohan studies science from 6 PM to 7:30 PM at home. Consider the tip of the minute’s hand of the wall clock. During the given time interval, what is its: (i) distance travelled, (ii) displacement, (iii) speed, and (iv) velocity. The length of the minute’s hand is 7 cm.
items.answer: Given: length of minute hand r = 7 cm. Time interval 6:00 PM to 7:30 PM = 1.5 hours = 90 min = 5400 s. Revolutions completed: 1.5 complete revolutions (the minute hand completes 1 revolution per hour). (i) Distance travelled: the tip traces the circumference of a circle, so distance = number of revolutions × circumference. Circumference = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm. Distance = 1.5 × 44 = 66 cm. (ii) Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between the initial and final positions of the tip. At 6:00 PM the minute hand points to 12 (top). At 7:30 PM the minute hand points to 6 (bottom). These two positions are at diametrically opposite ends of the clock face. Displacement = diameter = 2r = 2 × 7 = 14 cm (directed from 12 towards 6, i.e. vertically downward). Note: after 1 full revolution (at 7:00 PM) the tip returns to 12; in the remaining 30 min it moves to 6 — exactly diametrically opposite to the start. (iii) Speed = total distance / total time = 66/5400 = 0.0122 cm s-1 (or 11/900 cm s-1). (iv) Velocity = displacement / total time = 14/5400 = 0.002592... cm s-1 ≈ 0.0026 cm s-1 (directed from 12 to 6, vertically downward).

2. Isolate time t from the first equation v = u + at.
3. Simplify the resulting algebraic equation to eliminate t entirely.
Select the correct logical sequence:
items.answer: To derive the third kinematic equation, the initial crucial step is to rearrange the first equation to express time exclusively. Following this, this new expression for time must be carefully substituted directly into the second equation for displacement. Finally, the resulting complex expression is algebraically expanded and simplified to reach the final formula.

items.answer: When constructing any standard scientific graph, the mandatory first step is properly drawing the perpendicular axes and locating the origin. items.stem:
Identify the correct statements regarding the examples of motion in different dimensions:

items.answer: Movement strictly along a straight highway or straight train track is defined as one-dimensional motion. Therefore, stating a train exhibits two-dimensional motion is factually incorrect. Motion within a flat plane, like a planetary orbit, is two-dimensional. Movement freely through open space, like a flying bird, inherently represents complex three-dimensional motion.

items.answer: The precise distance a vehicle travels after brakes are engaged is mathematically governed by the third kinematic equation. items.stem: What is meant by describing the position of an object?
items.answer: Describing the position of an object involves specifying a fixed reference point, along with the distance and direction at any instant of time.
items.concept: Position depends on distance and direction

items.stem: Under what condition is an object said to be in a state of rest?
items.answer: An object is said to be at rest if its position with respect to a chosen reference point does not change over time.
items.concept: Rest as no change in position

items.stem: Define the term displacement of an object in motion.
items.answer: Displacement is defined as the net change in the position of an object between two given instants of time, possessing both magnitude and direction.

items.stem: State one difference between distance and displacement.
items.answer: Distance is the total path travelled requiring only a numerical value, whereas displacement is the net position change requiring both magnitude and direction.

items.stem: What is the SI unit of average velocity and average speed?
items.answer: The standard international unit for measuring both average speed and average velocity is metre per second, which is represented as m s-1 or m/s.

items.stem: Write the formula for calculating the average speed of an object.
items.answer: The average speed of a moving object is calculated by dividing the total distance travelled by the total time interval taken to cover it.

items.stem: What is meant by uniform motion in a straight line?
items.answer: Uniform motion in a straight line occurs when an object covers equal distances in exactly equal intervals of time, maintaining a completely constant speed.
items.concept: Uniform motion in a straight line

items.stem: Under what condition is the magnitude of average velocity equal to average speed?
items.answer: The magnitude of average velocity equals the average speed strictly when an object moves in a single straight line without turning back or changing direction.

items.stem: Define the average acceleration of an object over a time interval.
items.answer: Average acceleration is defined as the total change in the velocity of an object divided by the specific time interval during which it occurs.

items.stem: What is the SI unit of average acceleration?
items.answer: The SI unit of average acceleration is metre per second squared, which is mathematically represented as m s-2 or m/s² in scientific contexts.

items.stem: What causes the negative sign in acceleration when a vehicle brakes?
items.answer: The negative sign indicates that the acceleration is acting directly opposite to the direction of velocity because the magnitude of the velocity is rapidly decreasing.

items.stem: What would you observe about an object’s acceleration if its velocity is perfectly constant?
items.answer: If an object moves with a perfectly constant velocity along a straight line, you will observe that its average acceleration remains exactly at zero.

items.stem: What is the significance of the slope in a position-time graph?
items.answer: The slope of a line on a position-time graph is highly significant because it directly provides the magnitude of the average velocity of the object.

items.stem: What does a curved line on a position-time graph indicate?
items.answer: A curved line on a position-time graph clearly indicates that the velocity of the object is not constant, representing an accelerated or non-uniform motion.

items.stem: What does a perfectly straight line parallel to the time axis on a position-time graph represent?
items.answer: A perfectly straight line parallel to the time axis on a position-time graph represents a completely stationary object that remains entirely at rest over time.

items.stem: What is the significance of the area enclosed under a velocity-time graph?
items.answer: The area enclosed by the line on a velocity-time graph and the time axis accurately represents the total displacement of the object within that interval.

items.stem: What is the relationship represented by the first kinematic equation of motion?
items.answer: The first kinematic equation, v equals u plus at, mathematically relates final velocity, initial velocity, constant acceleration, and time interval for an object in motion.

items.stem: Write the kinematic equation that relates displacement, initial velocity, time, and acceleration.
items.answer: The primary kinematic equation relating displacement, initial velocity, time, and constant acceleration is formulated as s equals ut plus half at squared.

items.stem: Correct the statement: “Kinematic equations can be used for any type of accelerated motion.”
items.answer: These standard kinematic equations are uniquely valid only for straight-line motion where the acceleration remains completely constant throughout the chosen interval of time.

items.stem: What is uniform circular motion?
items.answer: Uniform circular motion occurs specifically when an object continuously moves along a circular path while maintaining a perfectly constant and unchanging overall speed.

items.stem: Why is uniform circular motion considered an accelerated motion despite constant speed?
items.answer: It is considered an accelerated motion because the direction of the object’s velocity continuously changes at every single point along the curved circular path.

items.stem: What is the direction of velocity of an object in uniform circular motion?
items.answer: The velocity of an object in uniform circular motion is always directed along the tangent drawn to the circular path at that specific point.

items.stem: Give the formula to calculate the average speed of an object completing one circular revolution.
items.answer: For one complete revolution, the average speed is calculated as two pi times the radius divided by the total time taken for the trip.

items.stem: What is the result of displacement when an athlete completes exactly one full round on a circular track?
items.answer: The resulting displacement becomes exactly zero because the athlete successfully returns to the original starting point, making the net change in position completely nil.

items.stem: Which ancient Indian text features the concept of calculating speed from distance and time?
items.answer: The comprehensive concept of calculating speed is featured prominently in mathematical texts from ancient India, specifically seen within the fifth-century treatise known as Aryabhatiya.

items.stem: How is instantaneous velocity different from average velocity?
items.answer: Average velocity measures position change over a large time interval, whereas instantaneous velocity specifically describes the velocity of an object at a precise, particular instant.

items.stem: What would happen to a marble moving in a circular ring if the ring is suddenly lifted?
items.answer: If the ring is suddenly lifted, the marble will immediately move away in a straight line corresponding to the tangent of its previous circular path.

items.stem: Give one example of motion in two dimensions from everyday life.
items.answer: A common everyday example of two-dimensional motion in a plane is a kicked football travelling through the air or a vehicle overtaking another car.

items.stem: What is the relationship between the slope of a velocity-time graph and acceleration?
items.answer: The steepness or slope of a straight line on a velocity-time graph directly determines how fast velocity changes, perfectly representing the object’s exact uniform acceleration.

items.stem: What is the scientific term for the acceleration caused by the Earth’s gravitational force?
items.answer: The specific acceleration experienced by freely falling objects due to the Earth’s gravitational pull is scientifically termed as acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g.

items.stem: Explain with an example how the magnitude of displacement can be zero even if the distance travelled is not zero.
items.answer: Displacement is the net change in an object’s position between its initial and final points, while distance is the total path length covered. If an athlete runs one complete round on a circular track and returns to the exact starting line, the total distance travelled equals the track’s circumference. However, because the initial and final positions are identical, the net change in position is zero. Therefore, the displacement is zero despite a significant non-zero distance being travelled by the athlete.

items.stem: Explain how the average velocity of an object can be zero while its average speed is non-zero, using a daily life example.
items.answer: Average velocity is calculated as total displacement divided by time, whereas average speed is total distance divided by time. If you travel from your home to school and return home along the same path, your total displacement is zero since your starting and stopping points are identical. Consequently, your average velocity for the entire trip is zero. However, your average speed will be non-zero because you covered a specific total distance going to the school and coming back during that time interval.

items.stem: Describe what is meant by average acceleration. State its SI unit and the condition under which it acts opposite to the direction of motion.
items.answer: Average acceleration is defined as the change in an object’s velocity divided by the time interval over which that change occurs. Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m s-2). Acceleration possesses both magnitude and direction. It acts opposite to the direction of motion when the magnitude of the object’s velocity is decreasing. For instance, when a driver applies the brakes to a moving car, the velocity decreases, resulting in negative acceleration acting in the direction opposite to the car’s movement.

items.stem: Draw a position-time graph for an object moving with a constant positive velocity. Explain how you can find the velocity from this graph.
items.answer: To find the velocity from this position-time graph, you must calculate the slope of the straight line. You can select any two distinct points on the graph, such as A and B. By drawing lines parallel to the axes, form a triangle. The vertical side represents the change in position, while the horizontal side represents the change in time. Dividing the position change by the time change gives the slope, which equals the object’s constant average velocity.

items.stem: Explain how you can calculate the displacement of an object moving with constant acceleration from its velocity-time graph.
items.answer: To calculate the displacement of an object from its velocity-time graph, you must determine the area enclosed by the velocity-time line and the time axis for the given time interval. For constant acceleration, the graph is a straight inclined line. The area under this line typically forms a trapezium. By dropping perpendiculars to the time axis from the initial and final time points, you can calculate the total area as the sum of a rectangle and a triangle, which equals the total displacement.

items.stem: Draw a velocity-time graph for an object that is slowing down with uniform acceleration. Explain what the slope of this graph indicates.
items.answer: The drawn graph shows a straight downward-sloping line, representing an object undergoing uniformly decreasing velocity. The slope of any velocity-time graph gives information about the rate at which velocity is changing with time, which is the acceleration. In this specific case, because the line slants downwards, the slope yields a negative mathematical value. This negative slope indicates that the acceleration acts in the opposite direction to the object’s movement, effectively acting as a retarding force that slows the object down.

items.stem: How does the shape of a position-time graph help us determine whether an object is stationary, moving with constant velocity, or moving with changing velocity?
items.answer: The shape of a position-time graph visually indicates the nature of an object’s motion. If the graph is a straight line parallel to the time axis, the object’s position is not changing, meaning it is stationary. A straight inclined line indicates that the object covers equal distances in equal time intervals, representing constant velocity. On the other hand, if the position-time graph is a curve, it shows that unequal distances are covered in equal intervals, which indicates changing velocity or accelerated motion.

items.stem: State the three kinematic equations for motion in a straight line with constant acceleration. Mention what each symbol represents.
items.answer: The three kinematic equations are v = u + at, s = ut + ½ at², and v² = u² + 2 as. In these mathematical expressions, ‘u’ represents the initial velocity of the moving object, and ‘v’ represents its final velocity at time ‘t’. The symbol ‘a’ denotes the constant acceleration experienced by the object, while ‘s’ stands for the total displacement covered during the given time interval ‘t’. These equations help predict the position and velocity of an object at any future time.

items.stem: Draw a diagram showing an athlete running on a circular track. Explain how the direction of velocity changes at different points on the track.
items.answer: When an athlete runs along a circular track, they are exhibiting uniform circular motion. The drawn diagram illustrates that the direction of the athlete’s velocity at any given instant is always directed along the tangent to the circle at that exact position. As the athlete progresses along the curved path, the tangential direction continuously shifts. Consequently, even if the athlete maintains a perfectly steady running speed, their velocity is constantly changing due to this endless alteration in their movement direction.

items.stem: Study the given position-time graph. (a) Which object, A or B, has a higher magnitude of velocity? (b) Justify your answer based on the features of the graph.
items.answer: (a) Object B definitely possesses a higher magnitude of velocity compared to object A. (b) In a position-time graph, the velocity of an object corresponds directly to the slope or steepness of its line. A steeper line signifies a greater rate of change in position over the same duration. Because line B is noticeably steeper than line A, object B covers a significantly larger displacement in the identical time interval. Therefore, object B operates at a higher velocity than object A.

items.stem: Explain why uniform circular motion is considered an accelerated motion even if the object is moving with a constant speed.
items.answer: In uniform circular motion, an object travels along a circular path with a constant speed. However, velocity is a physical quantity that requires both magnitude (speed) and direction. As the object moves along the circle, its direction of motion continuously changes at every single point along the path. Because the direction of velocity is constantly changing, the velocity itself is not constant. This continuous change in velocity with respect to time means that uniform circular motion is always an accelerated motion.

items.stem: Describe the activity using a ring and a marble to demonstrate the direction of velocity of an object moving in a circular path.
items.answer: Place a flat ring, like an adhesive tape ring, on a smooth surface and roll a marble so it rotates along the ring’s inner boundary. The marble undergoes circular motion. If you suddenly lift the ring, the marble stops moving in a circle and travels in a straight line instead. This straight-line path is tangential to the circular path at the exact point where the ring was removed. This activity demonstrates that the velocity’s direction in circular motion is always along the tangent.

items.stem: Define position and reference point. Why is it necessary to specify a reference point to describe motion?
items.answer: Position is the exact location of an object at any instant of time, specified by a distance and direction from a fixed point. A reference point is this chosen fixed location used as an origin to determine the object’s coordinates. Specifying a reference point is essential because motion is a relative concept. An object is considered in motion only if its position changes over time with respect to this specific reference point, otherwise, it remains at rest relative to that observer.

items.stem: What is the difference between average speed and average velocity? Why is average velocity considered a more complete description of an object’s motion?
items.answer: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time interval, possessing only magnitude. In contrast, average velocity is the net displacement divided by the time interval, requiring both magnitude and direction. Average velocity provides a more complete description of an object’s motion because it specifies how fast the position is changing and in which specific direction. Speed alone cannot indicate where the object is heading, making velocity crucial for understanding complex, real-world motions like navigating to a specific destination.

items.stem: Define uniform and non-uniform motion in a straight line. Give one example of each from everyday life.
items.answer: Uniform motion occurs when an object travels equal distances in equal intervals of time along a straight line. An example is a car driving steadily at exactly 60 km/h on an empty, straight highway. Non-uniform motion occurs when an object travels unequal distances in equal intervals of time, indicating changing speed. An example is a train departing from a station, where its speed continuously increases as it moves forward, or a bicycle slowing down when approaching a crowded intersection.
items.concept: Uniform motion in a straight line

items.stem: The given diagram shows an object dropped from a height. (a) Is the acceleration of this falling object constant or changing? (b) What is the direction of acceleration relative to its velocity?
items.answer: (a) The acceleration of the falling object remains perfectly constant throughout its descent. The velocity increases by precisely 9.8 m/s during every single successive second interval. (b) Since the magnitude of the object’s velocity is continually increasing as it falls downwards, the acceleration must be acting in the exact same direction as the object’s velocity. Both the velocity and this gravitational acceleration point vertically downwards towards the earth. This causes the object to speed up uniformly as it drops.

items.stem: What does the slope of a position-time graph represent? How will the slopes differ for a fast-moving and a slow-moving object?
items.answer: The slope of a position-time graph represents the rate of change of position, which is the magnitude of the object’s average velocity. It is calculated by dividing the change in position by the change in time. The steepness of this slope directly reflects the object’s speed. A fast-moving object covers more distance in less time, resulting in a much steeper slope on the graph. Conversely, a slow-moving object covers less distance in the same time, producing a flatter, less steep slope.

items.stem: The diagram below shows a velocity-time graph. (a) Identify the exact type of motion shown in this graph. (b) How can you calculate the displacement from this graph?
items.answer: (a) The graph displays uniform motion in a straight line, which means the object is travelling with a constant, unchanging velocity. Its acceleration is absolutely zero. (b) You can calculate the total displacement by determining the geometric area enclosed between the horizontal velocity line and the time axis for the chosen interval. Because the line is horizontal, this enclosed shape forms a simple rectangle. Multiplying the rectangle’s length (time interval) by its height (velocity magnitude) directly yields the total displacement.

items.stem: What is average acceleration? What does a negative sign in the value of average acceleration indicate?
items.answer: Average acceleration is the change in an object’s velocity divided by the time interval during which that change takes place. It measures how quickly the velocity of an object is altering. When calculating this value, a negative sign indicates that the acceleration acts in the direction opposite to the object’s initial velocity. In one-dimensional motion, this generally implies that the magnitude of the object’s velocity is decreasing over time, a scenario commonly experienced when a moving vehicle applies its brakes to stop.

items.stem: State the formula for the average speed of an object moving in a uniform circular path. Why is the displacement after one complete revolution zero?
items.answer: The average speed for uniform circular motion is calculated using the formula v = 2πR/T, where R is the radius of the circular path and T is the time taken to complete one full revolution. Displacement measures the shortest straight-line distance between the starting and ending positions. When an object completes exactly one revolution, it returns precisely to its original starting point. Because the initial and final positions are identical, the net change in position, and therefore the displacement, is strictly zero.

items.stem: What happens to an object’s speed and velocity during uniform circular motion? Why is this motion called an idealised model?
items.answer: During uniform circular motion, the object’s speed remains constant, meaning it covers equal distances along the circumference in equal time intervals. However, its velocity continuously changes because the direction of motion alters at every point on the circular path. This motion is called an idealised model because, in the real world, maintaining perfectly constant speed on a perfectly circular path without any external disturbances is extremely difficult. Yet, it forms the foundation for understanding complex real-world motions like planetary orbits.

items.stem: What physical quantity is represented by the area enclosed under a velocity-time graph? How is this area calculated for an object starting from rest with uniform acceleration?
items.answer: The area enclosed by the velocity-time graph and the time axis represents the total displacement covered by the moving object within that specific time interval. For an object starting from rest with uniform acceleration, the velocity-time graph is a straight line passing through the origin. The area bounded under this line forms a right-angled triangle. This displacement can be calculated by finding the area of this triangle, using the formula half multiplied by the base (time) and the height (final velocity).

items.stem: Draw a position-time graph showing an object that is stationary for some time and then moves with constant velocity. Why is the graph for a stationary object a horizontal line parallel to the time axis?
items.answer: The drawn graph begins with a horizontal segment, which denotes that the object’s position coordinate is not changing despite the passage of time. A stationary object simply remains exactly at its fixed location relative to the reference point. Therefore, as time values advance along the x-axis, the position value on the y-axis stays constantly identical. This mathematical relationship inherently produces a perfectly flat, horizontal line that runs parallel to the time axis on the coordinate graph.

items.stem: Compare distance and displacement with respect to direction dependence and their values when an object completely returns to its initial starting point.
items.answer: Distance is a scalar quantity that measures the total path length covered by an object and requires absolutely no direction for its description. Conversely, displacement is a vector quantity measuring the net positional change, heavily relying on a specified direction from origin. When an object completes a journey and returns precisely to its initial starting point, the total distance measured will be a large non-zero positive number. However, because the initial and final positions coincide, the net displacement becomes exactly zero.

items.stem: Draw a diagram of a merry-go-round showing a child’s circular path. If the child takes time T for one revolution of radius R, how do you find their average speed, and why is the velocity continuously changing?
items.answer: When a child rides a merry-go-round, they travel a total distance equal to the circle’s circumference (2πR) in one complete revolution taking time T. Their average speed is simply calculated using the formula v = 2πR/T. Although this calculated speed remains completely steady, the child’s velocity continuously changes. This occurs because velocity is a vector. As the merry-go-round rotates, the specific direction the child is facing and moving constantly shifts at every single point along the circular path.

items.stem: A student says that a car moving at a high constant speed of 100 km/h on a perfectly straight highway has zero acceleration. Is this correct? Justify using the concept of acceleration.
items.answer: Yes, the student’s statement is completely correct. Acceleration is scientifically defined as the rate of change of velocity over time. Velocity incorporates both the magnitude (speed) and the specific direction of the motion. If the car is moving on a perfectly straight highway at a steady 100 km/h, neither its speed nor its direction of travel is altering. Because there is absolutely no change in the car’s velocity, the calculated acceleration must be identically zero, regardless of how fast it moves.

items.stem: Renu claims that for motion in a straight line, the magnitude of average velocity can never be greater than the average speed. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
items.answer: Yes, I strongly agree with Renu’s claim. Average speed is calculated using the total distance travelled, while average velocity utilizes the net displacement. Displacement is fundamentally defined as the shortest straight-line path between initial and final positions. Therefore, the magnitude of displacement can only be equal to or less than the actual total distance covered. Because displacement can never exceed distance, the resulting average velocity magnitude can logically never be greater than the calculated average speed for any given time interval.

items.stem: Compare uniform motion and uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line with respect to the shape of their velocity-time graphs and their respective acceleration values.
items.answer: In uniform motion, an object maintains a constant speed and direction, meaning its acceleration value is entirely zero. The resulting velocity-time graph is a perfectly horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis. In uniformly accelerated motion, the object’s velocity increases or decreases by equal amounts in equal time intervals, resulting in a constant, non-zero acceleration value. Consequently, its velocity-time graph visually appears as a straight, inclined line sloping diagonally upwards or downwards depending on the velocity’s change.

items.stem: Why does the driver of a moving vehicle need to maintain a safe distance from the vehicle ahead? Explain in terms of negative acceleration and reaction time.
items.answer: When a driver suddenly notices a hazard and applies the brakes, the vehicle undergoes negative acceleration to slow down. However, stopping is not instantaneous. The total stopping distance heavily depends on the driver’s reaction time—the brief delay before pressing the brake—and the vehicle’s braking capacity. During the reaction time, the car continues moving rapidly forward at its initial velocity. Maintaining a safe distance guarantees enough available space for this combined reaction and braking distance, preventing devastating collisions with the vehicle ahead.

items.stem: Trace the sequential steps involved in determining the precise average velocity of a moving object from its position-time graph between two time instants t1 and t2.
items.answer: First, locate the two required time instants, t1 and t2, on the horizontal time axis. Next, trace vertically upwards to find their corresponding points, A and B, precisely on the position-time line graph. Draw horizontal lines from points A and B to the y-axis to read the position values s1 and s2. Finally, calculate the average velocity by dividing the change in position (s2 - s1) by the elapsed time interval (t2 - t1). Geometrically, this equals finding the line’s slope.

items.stem: (a) Differentiate between distance travelled and displacement? (b) Under what specific condition is the magnitude of average velocity equal to the average speed? (c) A boy walks 3 km East, then 4 km North in 2 hours. Calculate his total distance, displacement magnitude, average speed, and average velocity magnitude?
items.answer:
(a) Distance is the total path length covered by an object during its motion, whereas displacement is the shortest straight-line distance measured from the initial to the final position. Distance is a scalar, while displacement is a vector.
(b) The magnitude of average velocity equals the average speed only when an object moves in a single straight line in one direction without turning back.
(c) For the walking boy, the distance travelled is the sum of the two paths: 3 km + 4 km = 7 km.
His displacement magnitude is calculated using the Pythagorean theorem, since he turns North after going East:
Displacement = sqrt(3² + 4²) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 km.
Average speed is total distance divided by time: 7 km / 2 h = 3.5 km h-1.
Average velocity magnitude is displacement divided by time: 5 km / 2 h = 2.5 km h-1.

items.stem: (a) Define average acceleration and state its SI unit? (b) How do we determine the direction of acceleration for an object moving in a straight line? (c) A train starting from rest attains a velocity of 72 km h-1 in 5 minutes. Assuming uniform acceleration, find the acceleration and the distance travelled?
items.answer:
(a) Average acceleration is defined as the change in velocity of an object divided by the time interval over which that change occurs. Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m s-2).
(b) For straight-line motion, if the magnitude of velocity increases, acceleration acts in the same direction as the velocity. If the velocity decreases, acceleration acts opposite to the direction of velocity.
(c) For the train:
Initial velocity (u) = 0 m s-1
Final velocity (v) = 72 km h-1 = 72 × (5/18) = 20 m s-1
Time (t) = 5 minutes = 300 s
Acceleration (a) = (v - u)/t = (20 - 0)/300 = 1/15 m s-2 ≈ 0.067 m s-2
Using the equation for distance:
s = ut + ½at²
s = 0(300) + 0.5 × (1/15) × (300)²
s = 0.5 × (1/15) × 90000
s = 3000 m or 3 km.
The train travels 3 km.

items.stem: (a) Write the three kinematic equations for motion in a straight line with constant acceleration? (b) Why are these equations not applicable for an object moving in a circular path at a constant speed? (c) A car travelling at 90 km h-1 applies brakes, producing a constant acceleration of -0.5 m s-2. How far will it go before stopping?
items.answer:
(a) The three kinematic equations for motion in a straight line with constant acceleration are:
v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²
and v² = u² + 2as.
(b) These equations are valid only when acceleration remains constant in both magnitude and direction. In uniform circular motion, although the speed is constant, the direction of motion changes continuously. Consequently, the velocity and acceleration change direction at every single point, meaning acceleration is not constant, rendering these equations strictly invalid for circular paths.
(c) For the braking car:
Initial velocity (u) = 90 km h-1 = 90 × (5/18) = 25 m s-1
Final velocity (v) = 0 m s-1 (since it is brought to rest)
Acceleration (a) = -0.5 m s-2
Using the third equation v² = u² + 2as:
0 = (25)² + 2(-0.5)s
0 = 625 - s
s = 625 m.
The car travels 625 m before fully stopping.

items.stem: (a) What physical quantities are obtained from the slope and the area under a velocity-time graph? (b) How does the velocity-time graph for constant velocity differ from one showing constant acceleration starting from rest? (c) A motorboat starting from rest accelerates at 3.0 m s-2 for 8.0 s. Calculate its displacement?
items.answer:
(a) From a velocity-time graph, the slope of the line gives the object's average acceleration, indicating exactly how fast velocity changes with time. The area enclosed between the velocity-time graph line and the time axis represents the total displacement of the object over that specific time interval.
(b) A velocity-time graph representing constant velocity is a straight horizontal line parallel to the time axis, meaning the acceleration is zero. For constant acceleration starting from rest, the graph is a straight inclined line originating precisely from the origin, indicating a uniform increase in velocity.
(c) For the accelerating motorboat:
Initial velocity (u) = 0 m s-1
Acceleration (a) = 3.0 m s-2
Time (t) = 8.0 s
Displacement 's' is calculated using the equation:
s = ut + ½at²
s = (0 × 8.0) + (0.5 × 3.0 × (8.0)²)
s = 0 + (1.5 × 64)
s = 96 m.
The motorboat travels 96 metres.

items.stem: (a) Explain the concept of braking distance for a moving vehicle? (b) Why does a vehicle travelling at a higher initial velocity require a much longer distance to stop? (c) A driver travelling at 54 km h-1 spots a hazard. His reaction time is 0.5 s, after which brakes cause an acceleration of -5 m s-2. Find the total stopping distance?
items.answer:
(a) Braking distance is the physical distance a vehicle travels from the precise moment the brakes are applied until it completely stops.
(b) Using the kinematic equation v² = u² + 2as, when the final velocity v = 0, the distance is s = -u²/(2a). This clearly shows that stopping distance is directly proportional to the square of the initial velocity (u²). Therefore, a faster vehicle needs a significantly longer distance to stop safely.
(c) For the driver:
Initial speed (u) = 54 km h-1 = 54 × (5/18) = 15 m s-1
During the 0.5 s reaction time, the car moves uniformly:
Reaction distance = u × t = 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 m
Once brakes are applied (a = -5 m s-2):
0² = (15)² + 2(-5)s
0 = 225 - 10s
s = 22.5 m (braking distance)
Total stopping distance = Reaction distance + Braking distance = 7.5 + 22.5 = 30 m.

items.stem: (a) Distinguish between average speed and average velocity? (b) Can an object have a zero average velocity but a non-zero average speed? (c) Usha swims in a 90 m long pool. She covers 180 m in one minute by swimming from one end to the other and back along the same path. Find her average speed and average velocity?
items.answer:
(a) Average speed is a scalar quantity defined as the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken. It has only magnitude. Average velocity is a vector quantity defined as the total net displacement divided by the total time. It involves both magnitude and direction.
(b) Yes, an object can have zero average velocity and non-zero average speed. This occurs whenever an object returns exactly to its initial starting point. In this case, the total displacement becomes zero, making velocity zero, while the physical distance covered remains positive.
(c) For Usha's swim:
Total distance covered in one minute = 90 m (forward) + 90 m (return) = 180 m
Total displacement = 0 m (since she returns precisely to the starting end)
Total time (t) = 1 min = 60 s
Average speed = Total distance/time = 180 m / 60 s = 3 m s-1
Average velocity = Displacement/time = 0 m / 60 s = 0 m s-1

items.stem: A racing car has a uniform acceleration of 4 m s-2. What distance will it cover in 10 s after start?
items.answer:
Given: Uniform acceleration (a) = 4 m s-2.
Time (t) = 10 s.
The car starts from rest, so initial velocity (u) = 0 m s-1.
We need to find the distance covered, s.
Using the second equation of motion:
s = ut + ½at²
s = (0 m s-1)(10 s) + ½(4 m s-2)(10 s)²
s = 0 + ½ × 4 × 100 m
s = 200 m
The racing car will cover 200 metres in 10 seconds after starting.

items.stem: Usha swims in a 90 m long pool. She covers 180 m in one minute by swimming from one end to the other and back along the same straight path. Find her average speed and average velocity.
items.answer:
Total distance covered by Usha = 180 m.
Total time taken = 1 minute = 60 s.
Average speed = Total distance covered / Total time taken = 180 m / 60 s = 3 m s-1
Since Usha swims from one end to the other and back to her starting point along the same straight path, her initial and final positions are the same. Therefore, her total displacement = 0 m.
Average velocity = Total displacement / Total time taken = 0 m / 60 s = 0 m s-1
So, Usha's average speed is 3 m s-1 and her average velocity is 0 m s-1.

items.stem: During an experiment, a signal from a spaceship reached the ground station in five minutes. What was the distance of the spaceship from the ground station? The signal travels at the speed of light, that is 3 × 10^8 m s-1.
items.answer:
Time taken for the signal to reach = 5 minutes.
Converting time to seconds:
t = 5 minutes × 60 seconds/minute = 300 s
Speed of the signal (speed of light):
v = 3 × 10^8 m s-1
Distance (s) can be calculated using the formula distance = speed × time:
s = v × t = (3 × 10^8 m s-1)(300 s)
s = 900 × 10^8 m
s = 9 × 10^10 m (or 9 × 10^7 km)
The distance of the spaceship from the ground station was 9 × 10^10 metres.

items.stem: An artificial satellite is moving in a circular orbit of radius 42250 km. Calculate its speed if it takes 24 hours to revolve around the Earth.
items.answer:
Given, radius of the circular orbit (r) = 42250 km.
Time taken for one revolution (t) = 24 hours.
The distance covered in one revolution is the circumference of the orbit, C = 2πr.
C = 2 × π × 42250 km
Using π ≈ 3.14:
C ≈ 2 × 3.14 × 42250 km ≈ 265330 km
Speed (v) = Distance / Time = C / t
Speed (v) ≈ 265330 km / 24 hours ≈ 11055.42 km h-1
To convert to m s-1:
11055.42 km h-1 × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) ≈ 3070.95 m s-1

items.stem: A bus decreases its speed from 80 km h-1 to 60 km h-1 in 5 s. Find the acceleration of the bus.
items.answer:
Initial speed (u) = 80 km h-1.
Convert to m s-1:
u = 80 × (1000/3600) = 80 × (5/18) = 400/18 ≈ 22.22 m s-1
Final speed (v) = 60 km h-1.
Convert to m s-1:
v = 60 × (1000/3600) = 60 × (5/18) = 300/18 ≈ 16.67 m s-1
Time taken (t) = 5 s.
Acceleration (a) = (v - u)/t
Acceleration (a) = (16.67 m s-1 - 22.22 m s-1) / 5 s
Acceleration (a) = -5.55 m s-1 / 5 s = -1.11 m s-2
The acceleration of the bus is approximately -1.11 m s-2 (the negative sign indicates retardation).

items.stem: A person moves along the boundary of a square field of side 10 m in 20 s. What will be the magnitude of displacement of that person at the end of 2 minutes 20 seconds?
items.answer:
Given, side of square field = 10 m.
So, perimeter = 10 m × 4 = 40 m.
The person moves along the boundary in 20 s.
Total time = 2 × 60 s + 20 s = 140 s.
Since in 20 s the person moves 40 m, the distance covered in 1 s = 40/20 = 2 m.
Therefore, in 140 s the distance covered = 2 × 140 = 280 m.
Now, the number of rounds needed to cover 280 m along the boundary = Total distance / Perimeter = 280 m / 40 m = 7 rounds.
Hence, after 7 rounds the person will be back at the starting point, so the displacement will be zero.

items.stem: Neha swims in a 90 m long pool. She covers 180 m in one minute by swimming from one end to the other and back along the same straight path. Find the average speed and average velocity of Neha.
items.answer:
Given,
Total distance = 180 m
Total displacement = 0
Time taken (t) = 1 min = 60 s
We know that,
Average speed (Vav) = Total distance / Total time taken = 180 m / 60 s = 3 m/s
Average velocity (Vav) = Displacement / Total time taken = 0 / 60 s = 0 m/s

items.stem: A car decreases its speed from 80 km/h to 60 km/h in 5 seconds. Find the acceleration of the car.
items.answer:
Given,
Initial velocity (u) = 80 km/h = 80 × (5/18) = 22.22 m/s
Final velocity (v) = 60 km/h = 60 × (5/18) = 16.67 m/s
We know that,
Time (t) = 5 s
Acceleration (a) = (v - u)/t
Acceleration (a) = (16.67 - 22.22) m/s / 5 s = -1.11 m/s²

items.stem: Figure represents the speed-time graph for a particle. Find the distance covered by the particle between t = 10 min and t = 30 min.
items.answer:
We draw perpendicular lines from the 10-minute point and the 30-minute point to the time axis (see figure). The distance covered is equal to the area of the rectangle ABCD, and its value is
Area of ABCD = AB × BC
= (30 min - 10 min) × (10 km/h)
= 20 min × 10 km/h
= (20/60) h × 10 km/h
= 10/3 km ≈ 3.33 km

items.stem: A train starting from a railway station and moving with uniform acceleration, attains a speed 40 km/h in 10 minutes. Find its acceleration.
items.answer:
Given,
Initial velocity (u) = 0 (starting from rest)
Final velocity (v) = 40 km/h = 40 × (5/18) = 11.11 m/s
Time (t) = 10 minutes = 10 × 60 = 600 s
We know that,
Acceleration (a) = (v - u)/t
Acceleration (a) = 11.11 m/s / 600 s = 0.0185 m/s²

items.stem: Find the distance covered by a particle during the time interval t = 0 to t = 20 s for which the speed-time graph is shown in figure.
items.answer:
The distance covered in the time interval 0 to 20 s is equal to the area of the shaded triangle. So,
Distance = ½ × base × height
= ½ × (20 s) × (20 m/s)
= 200 m

items.stem: The average speed of a bicycle, an athlete and car are 18 km/h, 7 m/s and 2 km/min respectively. Which of the three is the fastest and which is the slowest?
items.answer:
18 km/h = 18 km / 1 h = 18000 m / 3600 s = 5 m/s
2 km/min = 2 km / 1 min = 2000 m / 60 s = 33.3 m/s
Thus, the average speeds of the bicycle, the athlete and the car are 5 m/s, 7 m/s and 33.3 m/s respectively. So, the car is the fastest and the bicycle is the slowest.

items.stem: A bus moves 30 km in 30 min and the next 30 km in 40 min. Calculate the average speed for the entire journey.
items.answer:
Given, the total time taken is 30 min + 40 min = 70 min
and the total distance travelled is 30 km + 30 km = 60 km.
The average speed is
Vav = 60 km / 70 min = 60 km / (70/60) h = 3600/70 km/h = 51.4 km/h

items.stem: A girl runs for 10 min at a uniform speed of 9 km/h. What should be the speed that she runs for the next 20 min, so that the average speed comes to 12 km/h?
items.answer:
Given, total time = 10 min + 20 min = 30 min.
The average speed is 12 km/h. Using s = vt, the distance covered in 30 min is
12 km/h × 30 min = 12 km/h × ½ h = 6 km
The distance covered in the first 10 min is
9 km/h × 10 min = 9 km/h × (1/6) h = 1.5 km
Thus, she has to cover 6 km - 1.5 km = 4.5 km in the next 20 min.
The speed required is
4.5 km / 20 min = 4.5 km / (20/60) h = 13.5 km/h

items.stem: It is estimated that the radio signal takes 1.27 seconds to reach the Earth from the surface of the Moon. Calculate the distance of the Moon from the Earth. Speed of radio signal = 3 × 10^8 m s-1 (speed of light in air).
items.answer:
Given,
time = 1.27 s
Speed = 3 × 10^8 m s-1
Distance = ?
As we know, using distance = speed × time, we get
Distance = 3 × 10^8 m s-1 × 1.27 s
= 3.81 × 10^8 m
= 3.81 × 10^5 km

items.stem: A particle moves 3 m north, then 4 m east and finally 6 m south. Calculate the magnitude of displacement.
items.answer:
As shown in the figure, let us consider the east-west direction along the x-axis and the north-south direction along the y-axis. Then AB, BC and CD represent the displacements of 3 m north, 4 m east and 6 m south respectively.
The net displacement is represented by AD.
Magnitude of net displacement:
s = AD = sqrt(AE² + ED²)
= sqrt(BC² + (CD - AB)²)
= sqrt((4)² + (6 - 3)²)
= sqrt((4)² + (3)²)
= sqrt(16 + 9) = sqrt(25) = 5 m

items.stem: An electric train is moving with a velocity of 120 km/h. How much distance will it cover in 30 s?
items.answer:
Constant velocity of train (v) = 120 km/h = 120 × (5/18) = 100/3 m/s
Time (t) = 30 s
Distance covered (s) = vt = (100/3) × 30 = 1000 m = 1.0 km
items.concept: Uniform motion in a straight line

items.stem: On a 120 km track, a train travels the first 30 km at uniform speed of 30 km/h. Calculate the speed with which the train should move rest of the track so as to get the average speed of 60 km/h for entire trip.
items.answer:
As the average speed of the train for the entire journey of s = 120 km is vav = 60 km/h,
the total time taken by the train to cover the journey is
t = s/vav = 120 km / 60 km/h = 2 h
Time taken to travel the first 30 km at a uniform speed of 30 km/h:
t1 = 30 km / 30 km/h = 1 h
Time for covering the remaining distance [120 - 30] = 90 km should be
t2 = t - t1 = (2 - 1) h = 1 h
Constant speed of the train for this part of the journey:
v2 = s2/t2 = 90 km / 1 h = 90 km/h

items.stem: A girl while riding a bicycle moves with the speed of 10 km/h for 2 hours and with the speed of 15 km/h in the next 3 hours. Find the total distance moved by her and her average speed.
items.answer:
Distance moved by the girl in time t1 = 2 h with a speed V1 = 10 km/h is given as
s1 = V1t1 = 10 × 2 = 20 km
and the distance moved by the girl in the subsequent time t2 = 3 h with speed V2 = 15 km/h is given as
s2 = V2t2 = 15 × 3 = 45 km
Total distance moved by the girl = 20 + 45 = 65 km
Her average speed for the entire journey is
Vav = Total distance / Total time = s/(t1 + t2) = 65/5 = 13 km/h

items.stem: A marble rolling on a smooth floor has an initial velocity of 0.4 m/s. If the floor offers a retardation of 0.02 m s-2, calculate the time it will take to come to rest.
items.answer:
Here initial velocity (u) = 0.4 m/s
final velocity (v) = 0
acceleration (a) = -0.02 m s-2
As per the relation v = u + at,
t = (v - u)/a
t = (0 - 0.4)/(-0.02)
t = -0.4/-0.02 = 20 s

items.stem: A cyclist completes 8 revolutions of a circular track of radius 98 m with a uniform speed in 40 minutes. Calculate the speed.
items.answer:
Here the number of revolutions completed by the cyclist is n = 8, the radius of the circular track is r = 98 m,
and the time is t = 40 min = 40 × 60 s = 2400 s.
Uniform speed of the cyclist:
v = Total distance / Total time = 2πrn / t
v = (2 × (22/7) × 98 × 8) / 2400
v = 4928 m / 2400 s ≈ 2.05 m/s

items.stem: A person moves a distance of 3 km towards east then 2 km towards north and then 3.5 km towards east. Find : (a) The distance covered by the person, and (b) the displacement of his motion.
items.answer:
As shown, AB, BC and CD represent the distances of 3 km east, 2 km north and 3.5 km east respectively.
(a) Net distance covered by the person = AB + BC + CD = (3 + 2 + 3.5) km = 8.5 km
(b) Net displacement:
AD = sqrt(AE² + ED²)
= sqrt((AB + CD)² + BC²)
= sqrt((3 + 3.5)² + (2)²)
= sqrt((6.5)² + (2)²)
= sqrt(42.25 + 4)
= sqrt(46.25) = 6.8 km

items.stem: Divya walked 2 km on a straight road and then walked back 1 km. Which of the two quantities involved in her walking is greater - the scalar or the vector?
items.answer:
Distance travelled by Divya = 2 km + 1 km = 3 km
Displacement = 2 km - 1 km = 1 km
Hence, distance, which is a scalar quantity, is greater than the displacement, which is a vector quantity.

items.stem: A child moving on a circular track of radius 40 m completes one revolution in 5 minutes. What is his (i) average speed (ii) average velocity in one full revolution?
items.answer:
Distance travelled in one revolution = 2πr = 2π × 40 m
Displacement in one revolution = 0
Time taken = 5 minutes = 5 × 60 s = 300 s
(i) Average speed = Distance / Time = (2 × π × 40) / (5 × 60) = 4π/15 m/s ≈ 0.84 m/s
(ii) Average velocity = Displacement / Time = zero

items.stem: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of diameter 200 m in 40 s. (a) What is the distance covered by the athlete in 2 minutes 20 s? (b) What is the magnitude of the displacement of the athlete at the end of 2 minutes 20 s?
items.answer:
Diameter of the circular track = 200 m.
Radius (r) = diameter / 2 = 200 m / 2 = 100 m
Time taken for one round = 40 s.
Distance covered in one round (circumference):
C = 2πr = 2 × π × 100 m = 200π m
Let us use π = 22/7:
C = 200 × 22/7 = 4400/7 m ≈ 628.57 m
Total time of motion = 2 minutes 20 s = (2 × 60) s + 20 s = 120 s + 20 s = 140 s
Number of rounds completed = Total time / Time for one round = 140 s / 40 s = 3.5 rounds
(a) Distance covered = Number of rounds × Circumference = 3.5 × 200π m = 700π m.
Using π = 22/7: Distance = 700 × 22/7 m = 100 × 22 m = 2200 m
(b) Magnitude of displacement: After 3 complete rounds, the athlete is back at the starting point, so displacement is zero for these 3 rounds. For the remaining 0.5 round (half a circle), the athlete moves from the starting point to a point diametrically opposite on the circular track. The shortest distance between these two points is the diameter of the circle.
Magnitude of displacement = Diameter = 200 m.

items.stem: A farmer moves along the boundary of a square field of side 10 m in 40 s. What will be the magnitude of displacement of the farmer at the end of 2 minutes 20 seconds from his initial position?
items.answer:
Side of square field = 10 m.
Perimeter = 4 × 10 = 40 m.
Time taken for one round = 40 s.
Total time = 2 minutes 20 seconds = (2 × 60) + 20 = 120 + 20 = 140 s
Number of rounds completed = Total time / Time for one round = 140 s / 40 s = 3.5 rounds
After 3 complete rounds, the farmer is at the starting point. After the next 0.5 round (half the perimeter = 20 m), the farmer will be at the diagonally opposite corner.
If the starting point is A, the diagonally opposite corner is C.
Displacement = AC = sqrt(AB² + BC²)
= sqrt((10)² + (10)²)
= sqrt(100 + 100)
= sqrt(200) = 10 sqrt(2) ≈ 14.14 m

items.stem: The brakes applied to a car produce an acceleration of 6 m s-2 in the opposite direction to the motion. If the car takes 2 s to stop after the application of brakes, calculate the distance it travels during this time.
items.answer:
Given: Acceleration (retardation) a = -6 m s-2 (negative as it is opposite to the motion).
Time taken to stop (t) = 2 s.
Final velocity (v) = 0 m s-1 (since the car stops).
Using the first equation of motion, v = u + at:
0 = u + (-6 m s-2)(2 s)
0 = u - 12 m s-1
So, initial velocity (u) = 12 m s-1.
Now, using the second equation of motion:
s = ut + ½at²
s = (12 m s-1)(2 s) + ½(-6 m s-2)(2 s)²
s = 24 m - 12 m = 12 m
The car travels 12 m during this time.

items.stem: A train starting from rest attains a velocity of 72 km h-1 in 5 minutes. Assuming the acceleration is uniform, find (i) the acceleration and (ii) the distance travelled by the train for attaining this velocity.
items.answer:
Initial velocity (u) = 0 (starts from rest).
Final velocity (v) = 72 km h-1 = 72 × (1000/3600) = 20 m s-1
Time (t) = 5 min = 5 × 60 s = 300 s
(i) Acceleration: Using v = u + at,
Acceleration (a) = (v - u)/t = (20 - 0) m s-1 / 300 s = 20/300 m s-2 = 1/15 m s-2 ≈ 0.067 m s-2
(ii) Distance travelled: Using v² - u² = 2as,
s = (v² - u²)/(2a)
= ((20 m s-1)² - (0)²) / (2 × (1/15) m s-2)
= 400 / (2/15) m
= 400 × 15/2 m
= 3000 m = 3 km

items.stem: Joseph jogs from one end A to the other end B of a straight 300 m road in 2 minutes 30 seconds and then turns around and jogs 100 m back to point C in another 1 minute. (a) What is Joseph's average speed from A to B? (b) What is Joseph's average velocity from A to B? (c) What is Joseph's average speed from A to C? (d) What is Joseph's average velocity from A to C?
items.answer:
(a) Average speed from A to B:
Distance (A to B) = 300 m.
Time taken (A to B) = 2 minutes 30 seconds = (2 × 60) + 30 = 150 s
Average speed (A to B) = Distance / Time = 300 m / 150 s = 2 m s-1
(b) Average velocity from A to B:
Displacement (A to B) = 300 m (since it is a straight road in one direction).
Time taken (A to B) = 150 s.
Average velocity (A to B) = Displacement / Time = 300 m / 150 s = 2 m s-1 in the direction from A to B.
(c) Average speed from A to C:
Distance (A to B) = 300 m. Distance (B to C) = 100 m.
Total distance (A to C) = 300 m + 100 m = 400 m
Time taken (A to B) = 150 s. Time taken (B to C) = 1 minute = 60 s.
Total time (A to C) = 150 s + 60 s = 210 s
Average speed (A to C) = Total distance / Total time = 400 m / 210 s = 40/21 m s-1 ≈ 1.90 m s-1
(d) Average velocity from A to C:
Displacement (A to C) = Displacement (A to B) - Displacement (C to B, since he turns back)
= 300 m (from A to B) - 100 m (from B to C towards A)
= 200 m in the original direction of A to B.
Total time (A to C) = 210 s.
Average velocity (A to C) = Total displacement / Total time = 200 m / 210 s = 20/21 m s-1 ≈ 0.95 m s-1 in the direction from A to B.

items.stem: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of diameter 49 m in 20 s. Calculate the distance covered and the displacement at the end of 30 s.
items.answer:
Here, diameter D = 49 m.
As the athlete completes one round of a circular track in a period T = 20 s, in time t = 30 s he will complete
n = 30/20 = 1.5 rounds.
Thus, he will be at point B, diagonally opposite to the initial position A.
Displacement = AB = D = 49 m
Distance covered = n(2πr) = n(πD)
= 1.5 × (22/7) × 49
= 231 m

items.stem: Abdul, while driving to school, computes the average speed for his trip to be 20 km h-1. On his return trip along the same route, there is less traffic and the average speed is 30 km h-1. What is the average speed for Abdul's entire trip?
items.answer:
Let the distance from home to school be 'd' km.
Time taken to go to school:
t1 = Distance / Average speed = d/20 hours
Time taken for the return trip:
t2 = Distance / Average speed = d/30 hours
Total distance for the entire trip = d (to school) + d (return) = 2d km
Total time taken for the entire trip = t1 + t2 = d/20 + d/30 hours
To add the times, find a common denominator (e.g. 60):
Total time = (3d + 2d)/60 = 5d/60 = d/12 hours
Average speed for Abdul's entire trip = Total distance / Total time
= 2d km / (d/12) hours
= 2d × 12/d km/h
= 2 × 12 km/h
= 24 km/h
The average speed for Abdul's entire trip is 24 km h-1.

items.stem: A motorboat starting from rest on a lake accelerates in a straight line at a constant rate of 3.0 m s-2 for 8.0 s. How far does the boat travel during this time?
items.answer:
Given:
Initial velocity (u) = 0 m s-1 (starts from rest).
Constant acceleration (a) = 3.0 m s-2.
Time (t) = 8.0 s.
We need to find the distance travelled, s.
Using the second equation of motion:
s = ut + ½at²
s = (0 m s-1)(8.0 s) + ½(3.0 m s-2)(8.0 s)²
s = 0 + ½ × 3.0 × 64 m
s = 1.5 × 64 m
s = 96.0 m
The boat travels 96.0 metres during this time.

items.stem: A ball is gently dropped from a height of 20 m. If its velocity increases uniformly at the rate of 10 m s-2, with what velocity will it strike the ground? After what time will it strike the ground?
items.answer:
Given:
Initial velocity (u) = 0 m s-1 (gently dropped means it starts from rest).
Distance, or height, (s) = 20 m.
Uniform acceleration due to gravity (a) = 10 m s-2 (downwards, taken as positive).
Let 'v' be the final velocity when it strikes the ground, and 't' be the time taken.
To find the final velocity, use the third equation of motion v² = u² + 2as:
v² = (0)² + 2(10 m s-2)(20 m)
v² = 0 + 400 m² s-2
v² = 400 m² s-2
v = sqrt(400) m s-1 = 20 m s-1
The ball will strike the ground with a velocity of 20 m s-1.
To find the time taken, use the first equation of motion v = u + at:
20 m s-1 = 0 + (10 m s-2)t
t = 20/10 s = 2 s
The ball will strike the ground after 2 seconds.

items.stem: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of diameter 200 m in 40 s. What will be the distance covered and the displacement at the end of 2 minutes 20 s?
items.answer:
Given, diameter of circular track (D) = 200 m
Radius of circular track (r) = 200/2 = 100 m
Time taken by the athlete for one round (t) = 40 s
Distance covered by the athlete in one round:
s = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 100 = 4400/7 m
Speed of the athlete:
v = Distance / Time = (4400/7) m / 40 s = 4400 / (40 × 7) m s-1
Therefore, distance covered in 140 s = Speed × Time
= [4400 / (40 × 7)] × (2 × 60 + 20)
= [4400 / (40 × 7)] × 140
= 2200 m
Number of rounds in 40 s = 1 round.
Number of rounds in 140 s = 140/40 = 3½
After taking start from position X, the athlete will be at position Y after 3½ rounds, as shown in the figure.
Hence, the displacement of the athlete with respect to the initial position at X is XY = diameter of circular track = 200 m.

items.stem: Abdul, while driving to school, computes the average speed for his trip to be 20 km h-1. On his return trip along the same route, there is less traffic and the average speed is 30 km h-1. What is the average speed for Abdul's trip?
items.answer:
Let the distance of Abdul's school from his residence be s km.
As during his trip from his residence to school his average speed is V1 = 20 km h-1,
in covering a distance s km he takes the time
t1 = s/V1 = s/20 h
Similarly, during the return trip he takes the time
t2 = s/V2 = s/30 h
Average speed for Abdul's entire trip:
Vav = Total Distance / Total Time = (s + s) / (t1 + t2) km/h
Vav = (s + s) / (s/20 + s/30) km/h
= 2s / (s/12) km/h
= 2 × 12 km h-1
= 24 km h-1

items.stem: A motorboat starting from rest on a lake accelerates in a straight line at a constant rate of 3.0 m s-2 for 8.0 s. How far does the boat travel during this time?
items.answer:
Given initial velocity of motorboat, u = 0
Acceleration of motorboat, a = 3.0 m s-2
Time under consideration, t = 8.0 s
We know that distance, s = ut + (1/2)at²
Therefore, the distance travelled by the motorboat
= 0 × 8 + (1/2) × 3.0 × 8²
= (1/2) × 3 × 8 × 8 m
= 96 m

items.stem: Joseph jogs from one end A to the other end B of a straight 300 m road in 2 minutes 30 seconds and then turns around and jogs 100 m back to point C in another 1 minute. What are Joseph's average speeds and velocities in jogging (a) from A to B and (b) from A to C?
items.answer:
Total distance covered from A to B = 300 m
Total time taken = 2 × 60 + 30 s = 150 s
Therefore, average speed from A to B = Total Distance / Total Time = 300/150 m s-1 = 2 m s-1
Therefore, velocity from A to B = Displacement AB / Time = 300/150 m s-1 = 2 m s-1
Total distance covered from A to C = AB + BC = 300 + 100 m = 400 m
Total time taken from A to C = Time taken for AB + Time taken for BC = (2 × 60 + 30) + 60 s = 210 s
Therefore, average speed from A to C = Total Distance / Total Time = 400/210 m s-1 = 1.904 m s-1
Displacement from A to C = AB - BC = 300 - 100 m = 200 m
Time taken for displacement from A to C = 210 s
Therefore, velocity from A to C = Displacement / Time = 200/210 m s-1 = 0.952 m s-1

items.stem: A driver of a car travelling at 52 km h-1 applies the brakes and accelerates uniformly in the opposite direction. The car stops in 5 s. Another driver going at 3 km h-1 in another car applies his brakes slowly and stops in 10 s. On the same graph paper, plot the speed versus time graphs for the two cars. Which of the two cars travelled farther after the brakes were applied?
items.answer:
PR and SQ are the speed-time graphs for the two given cars, with initial speeds 52 km h-1 and 3 km h-1 respectively (given in the figure).
Initial speed of car A = 52 km h-1 = 52 × (5/18) = 14.44 m s-1
Car A stops in 5 s, i.e. its final speed is zero at time t = 5 s. So the speed-time graph of car A is the straight line from (0 s, 14.44 m s-1) down to (5 s, 0).
Initial speed of car B = 3 km h-1 = 3 × (5/18) = 0.83 m s-1
Car B stops in 10 s, i.e. its final speed is zero at time t = 10 s. So the speed-time graph of car B is the straight line from (0 s, 0.83 m s-1) down to (10 s, 0).
The speed-time graphs of both cars A and B are drawn on the same axes.
The distance travelled after the brakes were applied equals the area under each speed-time graph:
Car A: ½ × 5 s × 14.44 m s-1 ≈ 36.1 m
Car B: ½ × 10 s × 0.83 m s-1 ≈ 4.2 m
Therefore car A, which was travelling at 52 km h-1, travelled farther after the brakes were applied.

items.stem: A ball is gently dropped from a height of 20 m. If its velocity increases uniformly at the rate of 10 m s-2, with what velocity will it strike the ground? After what time will it strike the ground?
items.answer:
Let us assume the final velocity with which the ball will strike the ground is v, and the time it takes to strike the ground is t.
Initial velocity of ball, u = 0
Distance or height of fall, s = 20 m
Downward acceleration, a = 10 m s-2
As we know that,
2as = v² - u²
v² = 2as + u² = 2 × 10 × 20 + 0 = 400
Final velocity of ball, v = 20 m s-1
The time is given by t = (v - u)/a, so the time taken by the ball to strike the ground is
(20 - 0)/10 = 20/10 = 2 seconds

items.stem: Figure shows the distance-time graph of three objects A, B and C. Study the graph and answer the following questions : (a) Which of the three is travelling the fastest? (b) Are all three ever at the same point on the road? (c) How far has C travelled when B passes A? (d) How far has B travelled by the time it passes C?
items.answer:
(a) Speed = Distance / Time.
Slope of graph = (Y-axis) / (X-axis) = Distance / Time.
Therefore, speed = slope of the graph. Since the slope of object B is greater than that of objects A and C, B is travelling the fastest.
(b) All three objects A, B and C never meet at a single point. Thus, they were never at the same point on the road.
(c) 7 square boxes = 4 km, so 1 square box = 4/7 km.
C is 4 blocks away from the origin, therefore the initial distance of C from the origin = 16/7 km.
Distance of C from the origin when B passes A = 8 km.
Thus, the distance travelled by C when B passes A
= 8 - 16/7
= (56 - 16)/7
= 40/7 = 5.714 km
(d) Distance travelled by B by the time it passes C = 9 square boxes
= 9 × 4/7
= 36/7 = 5.143 km

items.stem: A school bus starts from a student's house (point O), travels 2 km East to pick up another student (point A), then travels 3 km further East to reach the school (point B). In the evening, the bus travels back along the same route, dropping the second student at point A and then returning to the first student's house (point O). 1. What is the total distance covered by the bus in the morning to reach the school from the first student's house? 2. What is the magnitude of the displacement of the bus in the morning from the first student's house to the school? 3. What is the total distance covered by the bus for the entire round trip (from O to B and back to O)? 4. What is the magnitude of the displacement of the bus for the entire round trip?
items.answer:
1. Total distance in the morning = OA + AB = 2 km + 3 km = 5 km.
2. Magnitude of displacement in the morning = OB = 5 km (East).
3. Total distance for the entire round trip = (OA + AB) + (BA + AO) = 5 km + 5 km = 10 km.
4. Magnitude of displacement for the entire round trip = 0 km (since the initial and final positions are the same, point O).

items.stem: A postwoman starts her daily route from the main post office. She drives 4 kilometers straight north along Mahatma Gandhi Road to deliver a large parcel at a school. After dropping it off, she realizes she missed a delivery at a bakery located 1 kilometer south on the exact same road. She turns her van around and drives back to the bakery. After completing this delivery, she parks her van there to take a short lunch break before continuing her route. Her smartwatch tracks her daily physical activity, showing both the total path she covered and her current distance from her starting location. (a) Calculate the total distance travelled by the postwoman from the post office to the bakery. (b) Determine the magnitude of her displacement when she is resting at the bakery. (c) Can the magnitude of displacement ever be greater than the total distance travelled? Give a reason based on this scenario. (d) If she returns to the main post office at the end of the day, what will be her final displacement?
items.answer:
(a) The total distance travelled is the sum of the actual path lengths. She drove 4 km north and then 1 km south. The total distance is 4 km + 1 km = 5 km.
(b) Displacement is the net change in position from the starting point. She went 4 km north and then returned 1 km south, leaving her 3 km north of the post office. The magnitude of her displacement is 3 km.
(c) No, the magnitude of displacement can never be greater than the distance travelled. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between initial and final positions, while distance is the entire actual path taken, which in this case was longer due to turning back.
(d) If she returns to her starting point at the post office, her final displacement will be zero, because there is no net change between her initial position and her final position at the end of the day.

items.stem: During a summer sports camp, a coach is training young swimmers in a rectangular Olympic-sized pool that is 50 meters long. A young swimmer named Tara is asked to swim from one end of the pool to the other and immediately return to her starting point. She swims at a steady pace. It takes her exactly 40 seconds to reach the opposite end. She turns around without stopping and takes another 60 seconds to swim back to the starting edge, as she feels slightly tired. The coach records her timings on a clipboard to analyze her performance and explain the difference between how fast she swims and her effective progress. (a) What is the total distance covered by Tara during the entire swim? (b) Calculate Tara's average speed for the entire journey. (c) What is Tara's average velocity for the entire round trip? (d) Why is her average velocity different from her average speed in this scenario? (e) Is Tara's motion during the first 40 seconds uniform or non-uniform? Justify if she swims at a steady pace.
items.answer:
(a) The pool is 50 metres long. Tara swims to the other end (50 m) and back (50 m). The total distance covered is 50 m + 50 m = 100 m.
